summary_findings: The Hindi-Urdu-Punjabi sky is stratified in three visible layers, and the lexicographic record of 1834-1896 lets each be dated. (1) A SANSKRITIC layer: Platts (1884) and Fallon (1879) simply carry the twenty-seven nakṣatras over as Hindi headwords (kṛttikā, rohiṇī, mṛg, mūl, svāti...), and Maya Singh's Panjabi Dictionary (1895, s.v. nachhattar, p. 786) prints the whole list of twenty-seven for Punjabi as well - so it is recorded here once and not itemised. What matters is that in living rural speech these appear in Middle-Indic reflexes, not tatsama forms: Grierson's Bihar Peasant Life (1885, §1082, p. 271) gives the generic word as nakhat / nachhattr / nichhattr and the individual asterisms as Rohni, Mirgsira, Aradra, Punarbas, Pukh, Maggha, Hast or Hathiya, Bināti/Siwāti - and they function not as stars but as sixteen-to-thirteen-day agricultural seasons, personified (Hathi rāni, 'Queen Hathiya'). (2) A PERSO-ARABIC layer entering through Urdu and fully naturalised: s̤uraiyā and parvīn for the Pleiades, suhail for Canopus, jabbār and jauzā for Orion, ʻaiyūq for Capella, jadī and quṭbī tārā for the pole star, farqadān for the Guards of Ursa Minor, suhā for Alcor, gardānak for the Pointers, banātu'n-naʻsh for the Bear as bier-and-daughters, kahkashāṅ for the Milky Way, nasru'l-wāqiʻ and nasru'ṭ-ṭāʼir for Lyra/Aquila. (3) A FOLK layer, which is where the real vernacular invention is. The Pleiades are 'the crowded-together ones' (kacpaciyā, gicpiciyā, kachbachiyā), a 'cluster' or ear-drop (guchchā tārā, jhumkā), or a hen with chickens (baccē-wālī murġī, gagan ke baccē-wālī murġī - Shakespear 1834 marks this last Deccani). Ursa Major is a piece of furniture with thieves at it: palang tīn cor, 'the bedstead and three thieves' (Shakespear 1834 p. 1949, also Deccani per Harris; Platts and Fallon unmarked); in Punjabi it splits, the four-star bowl being palang-pāwe 'the legs of the bedstead' and the three-star handle traṅgaṛ 'the net' (Dames, Panjab N&Q II.522), while O'Brien's Multani Glossary (1881, p. 62) makes traṅgar the whole Bear and notes the same word for the upper part of Orion. Fallon's sāt sahelyoṅ kā jhūmkā, 'the ear-drop cluster of the seven girl-friends', is the Bear again. The Milky Way is an elephant's road (hāthī kī rāh) or Hasta's road (hathiyā kī rāh), God's court-house (Bhagwān kī Kachahrī), the gate of heaven (Surg Dwārī), a white garland (Sufed Bādhī), and in Multani/Derawali the wake of Noah's ark (Berā dā Ghās). Venus at dawn is 'the star of the light' (ujāle-kā tārā), bhurkā/bhalkā, and in the Panjab 'the galloping star' (Tapt Tārā). Comets are brooms (jhāṛū) and tailed stars (ket, dum kā tārā, puchhalwālā tārā, dumdār sitārā). NEGATIVE FINDINGS: no vernacular name for SIRIUS could be verified - Platts, Fallon and Shakespear have no entry for it, the Sanskrit Lubdhaka/Mṛgavyādha do not surface, and Fallon (p. 801) misglosses Arabic suhail as 'the dog star', a conflation of Canopus with Sirius that Platts and Shakespear do not share; no ANTARES (no qalb al-ʻaqrab in Platts), no ARCTURUS beyond Sanskrit svāti, no CASSIOPEIA, no separate name for the HYADES. RAJASTHANI is the real gap: no Marwari/Rajasthani star name could be verified from any public-domain source reached here (Panjab and North Indian Notes & Queries carry no Rajputana star note; Fallon's Māṛ. tags never fall on a star word), and the modern Rajasthani lexicography that would settle it (Lalas) is in copyright - so no Rajasthani entry is claimed. Punjabi is thinly but genuinely attested (Maya Singh; Dames; Jukes; Chaina Mall of Ambala), Bhojpuri/Magahi rural usage is well attested through Fallon and Grierson and is entered here under 'Hindi' with the dialect named in region.

entries.region: Hindustani generally; recorded without regional restriction by Platts, Fallon and Shakespear
entries.usage_note: Built on the Hindi echo-compound kac-pac 'jumbled, crowded together' with the agent suffix -iyā; it is a descriptive nickname for the huddled cluster, not a reflex of Kṛttikā. Still current: McGregor, Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary (1993), p. 155, has कचपचिया नक्षत्र and Braj/Awadhi कचपची.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. kaćpaćiyā, p. 818
entries.quote: H کچپچيا कचपचिया kaćpaćiyā [kaćpać, q.v.+iyā = S. इकः], s.m. lit. 'Crowded together'; the Pleiades.
entries.notes: Platts prints both Devanagari and the Urdu script (Nastaʿlīq in the original type); both are given above in that order. Corroborated by Shakespear, A Dictionary, Hindustani and English (1834), s.v. kachpach-iyā, p. 1327, and by Fallon's variant kachbach'iyā (separate entry).

entries.usage_note: A phonetic doublet of kaćpaćiyā with initial g-; the two forms sit on different pages of Platts and evidently belong to different speech areas, though he marks neither.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. gić-pićiyā, p. 898
entries.quote: H گچپچيا गिचपिचिया gić-pićiyā [gic-pić = gać-pać, q.v.+Prk. इओ = S. इकः], s.m. The Pleiades.
entries.notes: Also in Shakespear (1834), s.v. gich-pichiyā, p. 1436, printed there in the Urdu script only: گچ پچيا.

entries.region: Hindustani generally (Fallon's dictionary is explicitly one of spoken idiom)
entries.usage_note: Fallon's spelling with -b- suggests contamination from bacca 'child/young one', which is also the base of the competing 'hen and chickens' name for the same cluster.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. kachbach'iyā, p. 917
entries.quote: H کچ بچيا कचबचिया kachbach'iyā , n. m. The Pleiades.
entries.notes: Competing form; see kaćpaćiyā and gić-pićiyā.

entries.usage_note: The commonest folk image for the cluster across Eurasia; here attached to the ordinary Hindi word for a young of any creature. Platts prints the compound in roman only, under the Devanagari/Urdu headword बच्चा / بچا.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. baććā, p. 135
entries.quote: baćće-wālī murg̠ī, s.f. lit. 'Hen with chickens'; the Pleiades.
entries.notes: name_native is left null because Platts gives no script form for the compound itself. Fallon, p. 230, s.v. bachchah, likewise glosses it only as 'The constellation of the Pleiades'. The expanded form with gagan is entered separately.

entries.region: marked dakh. (Deccani) by Shakespear; unmarked in Platts and Fallon, so also northern
entries.literal_meaning: 'the hen and chickens of the sky'
entries.usage_note: The fuller form of the preceding, with gagan 'sky' prefixed. Shakespear's dakh. tag is a genuine regional flag: several of these furniture-and-farmyard sky names reach him through Deccani Urdu.
entries.citation: John Shakespear, A Dictionary, Hindustani and English, 3rd ed. (London, 1834), s.v. gagaṇ, p. 1451
entries.quote: گگن کي بچي والي مرغي gagaṇ ke bachche wālī murg̠ẖ-ī (dakh.) The pleiades.
entries.notes: Shakespear prints the Urdu script only. Platts, p. 910, gives the same phrase in roman under गगण / گگن without any regional mark: 'gagaṇ-ke baćće-wālī murg̠ī, "The hen and chickens of the sky," the Pleiades'; Fallon, p. 1001, has it under gag'an.

entries.usage_note: guććhā is the ordinary word for a bunch of flowers or fruit, a tassel, a skein; the Pleiades are simply 'the bunch'. Fallon gives the Arabic ʻaqd-i-suraiyā ('the necklace of the Thurayyā') as its equivalent, showing the two layers translating each other.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. guććhā, p. 898
entries.quote: guććhā tārā, s.m. The Pleiades
entries.notes: Headword printed by Platts as गुच्छा / کچها. Fallon, p. 991, s.v. guch'chhā: 'guchchā tārā; A. aqd-i-suraiyā. (Ast.) Pleiades.' The compound itself is printed in roman by both, hence name_native null.

entries.usage_note: Platts classes it H (Hindi), from Sanskrit bahulāḥ, an old alternative name for the Kṛttikās; his adjectival entry bahul (p. 190) even preserves the sense 'born under the Pleiades'.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. bahulā, p. 190
entries.quote: H بہلا बहुला bahulā [S. बहुलास्], s.m. The Pleiades; name of a people.
entries.notes: Links to the Sanskrit database entry bahula (Bahulā, alias of Kṛttikā).

entries.usage_note: The central Arabic star name naturalised in Urdu, also as a woman's given name. The extended form ʻaqd-i-s̤uraiyā, 'the necklace of the Thurayyā', is what Fallon offers as the Arabic equivalent of Hindi guchchā tārā.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. s̤uraiyā, p. 368
entries.quote: A ثريا s̤uraiyā (from ثرو), s.m. The Pleiades ( = ʻaqd-i-s̤uraiyā).
entries.notes: Platts prints no Devanagari for Arabic-origin headwords, so only the Urdu script is given. Also Fallon, p. 461 ('surai'yā, aqd-i-suraīyā ... The Pleiades (jhumkā)'), and Shakespear, p. 599. A Panjab list of Arabic/Persian sky names (Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II, note 521, p. 84) gives it as 'Ssvayyá' [Thurayyā], 'diminutive of suru, plentiful, rich'.

entries.usage_note: The Persian counterpart of s̤uraiyā, equally at home in Urdu and equally common as a woman's name.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. parvīn, p. 258
entries.quote: P پروين parvīn , s.m. The Pleiades.
entries.notes: Also Fallon, p. 356, and Shakespear, p. 406. Panjab Notes and Queries II.521 (p. 84) records the Panjab Persian usage as 'Parvin or Paran'.

entries.usage_note: A strongly Punjabised reflex of Kṛttikā. The dictionary's second sense - a jewel in a nose-ring - repeats exactly the double life of Hindi jhumkā (ear-drop / star-cluster) and of bhalkā (morning star / gold star on a nose-ring): the same ornament vocabulary is used for both the sky and the face.
entries.citation: Bhai Maya Singh, The Panjabi Dictionary (Lahore, 1895), s.v. kirhkaṭí, p. 617
entries.quote: KIRHKAṬÍ ਕਿਰ੍ਹਕਟੀ s. f. The Pleiades; a jewel in a nose ring.
entries.notes: Gurmukhi as printed. This is the only Punjabi Pleiades name found in Maya Singh.

entries.usage_note: An aetiological tale rather than a name: the seventh sister is left out of the sharing of a sesame seed and so sits a little apart in the sky. Recorded from Sitapur. It explains a naked-eye fact - the cluster's outlier - and shows that the 'seven sisters' reading of the Pleiades is independently present in Awadhi village lore alongside the Sanskrit six Kṛttikās.
entries.citation: G. H. Roberts, 'Oudh - The Pleiades - Popular astronomy', Indian Notes and Queries [late Panjab Notes and Queries], vol. IV (1886-87), note 566
entries.quote: The Pleiades were seven sisters. It happened on a day that one of them found a seed of the til (sesamum). She divided it among six, the seventh sat behind her and was forgotten. That is how she takes her place just a little apart from the others in the sky.
entries.notes: No vernacular name is given in the note, hence name_roman is descriptive. Cited by note number, the standard locator for this journal.

entries.region: marked dakh. (Deccani) by Shakespear on Harris's authority; unmarked in Platts and Fallon
entries.usage_note: The single best folk name in the whole file: the four-star bowl is a charpoy and the three handle stars are thieves creeping up on it. R. C. Temple (Panjab Notes and Queries II.83) thought the image reached Hindustani from Turki, where the Qazaq name is likewise 'the seven thieves' who try to steal a horse from the Little Bear.
entries.citation: John Shakespear, A Dictionary, Hindustani and English, 3rd ed. (London, 1834), s.v. palang, p. 1949
entries.quote: پلنگ تين چور palang tīn chor (bedstead and three thieves), Charlesʼs wain (dakh. Harris).
entries.notes: Shakespear alone prints the phrase in the Urdu script. Platts, p. 268, s.v. palang (पलंग / پلنگ): 'palang tīn ćor, s.m. "The bed and three thieves," Charles's wain' - unmarked, i.e. northern too. Fallon, p. 366, adds the gloss 'S. सप्तऋषि', equating it with the saptarṣi.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the bell-shaped ear-drop'; in full 'the ear-drop of the seven girl-friends'
entries.usage_note: jhumkā is the pendant cluster of an ear-ring; applied to the sky it names both the Bear and the Pleiades, which is a genuine ambiguity in the sources and not a slip - Platts gives both senses in one entry. The full phrase sāt sahelyoṅ kā jhūmkā ('the seven girl-friends') fixes it on the Bear.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. jhum'kā, p. 499
entries.quote: H جهمکا झुमका jhum'kā, jhūmkā , n. m. 1. A cluster; a bunch of flowers or fruit. 2. The bell-shaped pendant of an earring. 3. (sāt sahelyoṅ kā jhūmkā) Charles's wain; Ursa major. 4. A flower; Gloriosa superba.
entries.notes: Independently confirmed for Urdu from the Panjab: L. Whyte King's list gives 'Urdu; jhamakkā, a cluster' for the Great and Lesser Bear, with the editor R. C. Temple adding '[This last is more commonly sāt sahelion ké jhamkā, the cluster of seven maidens.]' - Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Feb. 1885), note 521, p. 84. Platts, p. 407, lists the same word for 'Charles's Wain, Ursa Major; the Pleiades'.

modern_star.common_name: the Great Bear / the Little Bear

entries.usage_note: A calque, almost certainly of Arabic ad-dubb al-akbar / al-aṣghar rather than of English, since Fallon himself glosses sapt-rishī with 'A. dub-i-asgar'. The word rīchh is the inherited Indo-Aryan reflex of Sanskrit ṛkṣa, which in Sanskrit already meant both 'bear' and 'star' - so the calque lands on a word that was etymologically waiting for it.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. rīchh, p. 722
entries.quote: H ريچهـ रीछ rīchh; E. bhālū , n. m. S. ऋक्ष Pr. richchho. A bear. Baṛā rīchh; Sant. buṛhī parkom, Ursa major. Chhoṭā rīchh. Ursa minor.
entries.notes: Fallon repeats the equation at p. 703, s.v. rish'ī: 'sapt-rishī; H. baṛā rīchh; A. dub-i-asgar. lit. the seven saints. (Ast.) Ursamajor; Charles's Wain.' R. C. Temple reprints Fallon's data in Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II, note 83, p. 13. Fallon's 'Sant. buṛhī parkom' is a Santali (Munda, not Indo-Aryan) form and is not claimed here.

entries.region: Urdu, from Arabic; reported as the usual name among educated Muslims in the Panjab
entries.usage_note: The classical Arabic reading: four stars form the naʻsh, a bier, and the three ahead of it are the mourning daughters. Structurally identical to palang tīn ćor - four stars of furniture, three figures at them - which is why the two coexist so easily.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. banāt, p. 168
entries.quote: banātuʼn-naʻsh, s.m. The constellation of the Greater or Lesser Bear (consisting of seven stars, four of which are conceived to bear the resemblance of a naʻsh or bier, and the remaining three to be the banāt or daughters preceding it).
entries.notes: name_native gives only the headword بنات as Platts prints it; the compound itself he gives in roman. M. Longworth Dames, Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Feb. 1885), note 522, p. 84: 'Educated Musalmans in the Panjáb generally use the name Bindtu'n-na'sh and not Dubb-i-Akbar' [OCR: Bināt-]. He adds that on his informant's usage dubb-i-akbar means the four stars and dubb-i-aṣghar the three, not the Little Bear.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major - the four stars of the bowl

modern_star.common_name: the bowl of the Big Dipper
modern_star.bayer: α, β, γ, δ Ursae Majoris

entries.usage_note: The Punjabi version cuts the asterism in two and names the halves separately - the four bowl stars as the four legs of a charpoy, the three handle stars as a net. Dames notes the identical Balochi usage khaṭ-phāḍhagh, 'the legs of the bedstead'.
entries.citation: M. Longworth Dames, 'Names for the Great Bear', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Feb. 1885), note 522, p. 84
entries.quote: Panjabi: As in Balochi the four stars are called palang-pāwe, the legs of the bedstead. The three stars are called trangar, the net. This is the usage of the Jhang District.
entries.notes: Quoted with the OCR's evident misreadings of long vowels normalised only in the diacritics; wording and word-order are Dames's. Roman only in the source, so name_native is null.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major - the three stars of the handle (and the whole constellation)

modern_star.common_name: the handle of the Big Dipper; by extension the whole Dipper

entries.region: Multan and Dera Ghazi Khan (Multani/Saraiki); Jhang District
entries.literal_meaning: 'a wide-meshed net for carrying straw or fodder on pack animals'
entries.usage_note: A working object of the western Punjab plains - the loose net slung over a camel or donkey to carry straw - read into the sky. O'Brien makes it the whole Bear; Dames restricts it to the three handle stars and adds that the same word names the upper part of Orion, so it is a shape-word, not a fixed constellation name.
entries.citation: E. O'Brien, Glossary of the Multani Language compared with Punjábi and Sindhi (Lahore, 1881), s.v. trangar, p. 62
entries.quote: TRANGAR, s. m. - 1, a net of large meshes in which straw, grass, leaves, &c., are packed, to be loaded on camels, horses or donkeys; 2, the Great Bear constellation.
entries.notes: Dames, Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II, note 522, p. 84: 'O'Brien, Multání Glossary, s. v. trangar, gives trangar as the name of the Great Bear, but I believe it refers only to the three stars. The upper part of Orion is also called trangar.' The Orion application is entered separately.

entries.sky_object: Orion (the upper part of the figure)
entries.region: Jhang District and Multan, western Punjab
entries.usage_note: The same net-word applied to a second star-group. Which part of Orion is meant is not specified beyond 'the upper part', so the identification is deliberately loose here.
entries.citation: M. Longworth Dames, 'Names for the Great Bear', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Feb. 1885), note 522, p. 84
entries.quote: The upper part of Orion is also called trangar.
entries.notes: confidence disputed because 'the upper part of Orion' is not resolved to named stars; it may be the shoulders (Betelgeuse-Bellatrix) with the head, or the whole quadrilateral read as a net.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the forgotten one' (from Arabic sahw 'to be forgetful, to be overlooked')
entries.usage_note: The Arabic naked-eye test star, the faint companion of Mizar, taken into Urdu with its etymology intact - it is 'the one you overlook'. This is the exact functional counterpart of Sanskrit Arundhatī, likewise the tiny companion pointed out as a test.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. suhā, p. 704
entries.quote: A سہا suhā (v.n. fr. سہو 'to be forgetful,' &c.), s.m. A small dim star in the tail of Ursa Major.
entries.notes: Fallon, p. 799, s.v. su'hā, has the same: '(Ast.) The small star in the tail of the Great Bear.' The Sanskrit-side link is arundhati (Alcor).

entries.literal_meaning: diminutive of gardān 'turner, that which turns'
entries.usage_note: Named for their function: the two stars that swing round the pole and point to it.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. gardānak, p. 903
entries.quote: P گردانك gardānak (gardān+dim. aff. ak = S. क), s.f. The pointers (two stars in the Great Bear).
entries.notes: Also Shakespear (1834), p. 1441, in the same words. Identification as Dubhe and Merak is the standard sense of 'the Pointers' and is not stated by Platts.

entries.usage_note: The Iranian name of the Bear, reported in the Panjab beside the Arabic ones; Dames follows Max Müller in equating it etymologically with Sanskrit saptarṣi.
entries.citation: M. Longworth Dames, 'Names for the Great Bear', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Feb. 1885), note 522, p. 84
entries.quote: Persian. Haftwarang, from the Zend Haftoiring, which is equivalent, according to Max Müller, to the Sanskrit Saptarshi.
entries.notes: Reported as Persian in Panjab use rather than as a Punjabi word; register is vernacular in the sense used here (Perso-Arabic astronomical vocabulary current in the region). Roman only in the source.

entries.usage_note: The inherited Sanskrit name, retained unchanged; Platts and Fallon both file it as the standard learned equivalent of 'Charles's Wain'. Individual members keep their Sanskrit names in Hindi too: Platts s.v. marīćī (p. 1027) and vaśishṭh (p. 1194) each identify the sage with one of the seven stars.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. sapta, p. 634
entries.quote: The seven great saint-sages of the Hindūs; the seven principal stars in the constellation of Ursa Major (supposed to represent the seven sages), Charles's Wain
entries.notes: Recorded to mark the sanskritic layer explicitly; the analytic interest is in the folk names that compete with it.

entries.usage_note: The Arabic al-jady, the same word as the zodiac sign Capricorn, used for the pole star itself - a name that pins the star rather than the constellation.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. jadī, p. 378
entries.quote: A جدي jadī , s.m. A kid; a young he-goat; the sign Capricorn; the star a of Ursa minor, the pole-star.
entries.notes: Platts's next entry, جدي judai, is the diminutive, glossed simply 'The pole-star'.

entries.usage_note: A hybrid: Arabic quṭb 'pivot, pole' with the Indic word tārā 'star'. The naked Arabic quṭb alone is also used for the pole star (Platts p. 792; Fallon p. 888).
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. quṭbī, p. 792
entries.quote: P قطبي qut̤bī (rel. n. fr. qut̤b), adj. Of or relating to the north pole; polar: — qut̤bī tārā, s.m. The polar star.
entries.notes: Platts prints only the headword قطبي in script; the compound is roman. Still standard modern Hindi/Urdu (McGregor 1993, p. 204, s.v. क़ुतुब).

entries.region: Hindustani generally; the ritual is reported for Punjabi Hindus
entries.usage_note: Fallon's headword form dhurū is the vernacular reduction of Sanskrit dhruva, and he equates it directly with Arabic quṭb - the two layers glossing each other on one line. Ethnographically the star carries a vow: a Punjabi Hindu who salutes Dhrū for forty nights with his turban round his neck is said to learn of his death forty days in advance and to be joined to Dhrū's world after it.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. dhur'ū, p. 656
entries.quote: H دهرو धुरू dhur'ū; A. qutb , n. m. S. ध्रुव Pole (of the earth). Dhurū tārā. The polar star.
entries.notes: The forty-night vow: Chaina Mall, 'Pole Star - Dhru', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II, note 735. Platts, p. 543, gives the tatsama dhruv / dhruv-tārā. The Dhruva legend as told in the North-Western Provinces is summarised by Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), I. 24-25.

modern_star.common_name: Kochab and Pherkad, the Guards of the Pole

entries.usage_note: The Arabic al-farqadān, the pair that circles close to the pole. Shakespear (1834, p. 1258) muddles them as 'Two stars near the pole, the greater and lesser bears'; Platts has the identification right.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. farqadān, p. 779
entries.quote: A فرقدان farqadān , s.m. dual (of فرقد farqad, 'a calf'), Two bright stars in Ursa Minor near the pole-star.
entries.notes: Identification with β and γ UMi is the standard sense of al-farqadān; Platts says only 'two bright stars in Ursa Minor near the pole-star'.

entries.usage_note: Arabic al-jabbār, the giant - one of the two Arabic names of Orion that Urdu inherits. Platts files it in the same entry as the divine epithet 'Omnipotent', which is how the word is otherwise met in Urdu.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. jabbār, p. 375
entries.quote: A جبار jabbār (superl. or intens. fr. جبر), adj. & s.m. Omnipotent, mighty; — a conqueror; a revenger; a tall palm tree; Orion.
entries.notes: Also Shakespear (1834), p. 611. The Panjab list in Panjab Notes and Queries II.521 (p. 84) gives 'Orion. Arabic: An-nasaq, the row; al Jabbár, the giant.'

entries.usage_note: In Urdu jauzā covers both the zodiac sign Gemini and the constellation Orion - the classical Arabic ambiguity carried over whole. Fallon (p. 1072) gives it as the Arabic equivalent of Hindi mithun, Gemini.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. jauzā, p. 397
entries.quote: A جوزا jauzā , s.m. The sign Gemini; — Orion.
entries.notes: Also Shakespear (1834), p. 647, in identical terms.

modern_star.common_name: the Orion region - stag and hind, with a hunter nearby

entries.region: North-Western Provinces (Mirzapur/Saharanpur region; recorded by Pandit Ram Gharib Chaube for Crooke's journal)
entries.usage_note: A children's sky-name taught by mothers, with a Brahmā-and-Purvacitti pursuit myth attached in which Śiva takes the form of the Ārdrā asterism to help the hind. The living folk survival of the Vedic Mṛga/Prajāpati story, still located in Orion.
entries.citation: Pandit Ram Gharib Chaube, 'The Harina Harin Stars', North Indian Notes and Queries, vol. V (1895-96), note 517
entries.quote: Hindu mothers teach their children to point to the sky as they say these stars are the Stag and the Hind. Near them is a constellation which looks like a hunter armed with a bow and arrows.
entries.notes: confidence disputed: the note names no individual stars. The location in Orion is secured by the myth's use of the Ārdrā asterism (Betelgeuse) as Śiva's form; on the Sanskrit precedent the 'hunter with a bow and arrows' would be the Belt-as-arrow with Sirius as Mṛgavyādha the hunter, but the note does not say so, and no vernacular name for that figure is given.

entries.literal_meaning: Arabic Suhayl, diminutive-form of sahl 'level, easy'
entries.usage_note: The second-brightest star and, like Agastya, a low southern star whose heliacal rising is a season marker. It has entered Hindi verse: McGregor records सुहेल suhel as Avadhi for Canopus.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. suhail, p. 707
entries.quote: A سہيل suhail , corr. suhel (v.n. dim. form fr. سہل; see sahl), s.m. The star Canopus.
entries.notes: COMPETING IDENTIFICATION: Fallon, p. 801, s.v. suhail', suhel, glosses it 'The dog star', i.e. Sirius. That is an error - Platts (1884), Shakespear (1834, p. 1131) and Fallon's own entry at p. 115 (s.v. agas'ti, 'The star Canopus; Argo Navis (A. suhail...)') all make it Canopus. Recorded here because it is the only place in these dictionaries where Sirius is even approached.

entries.region: Bihar (Bhojpuri- and Magahi-speaking districts); the couplet is ascribed to the peasant weather-prophet Ghāgh
entries.usage_note: Not a learned citation but a farmer's calendar marker: the heliacal rising of Canopus, paired with the flowering of kās grass, announces that the rains are over. This is the Sanskrit Agastya name doing agricultural work in a peasant couplet.
entries.citation: G. A. Grierson, Bihar Peasant Life (Calcutta, 1885), §1091, p. 283
entries.quote: Uge agast ban phule kás, / Ab náhin barkha ke as. — The appearance of the star Canopus and the flowering of the kás grass in the forest are signs of the end of the rains.
entries.notes: Grierson prints the couplet in Devanagari above the transliteration; the Devanagari is badly mangled in the scanned text, so only his transliteration and translation are quoted and name_native is left null.

entries.usage_note: One of the very few individual stars for which Platts gives a precise positional identification, down to the Bayer letter.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. ʻaiyūq, p. 768
entries.quote: A عيوق ʻaiyūq , s.m. The star Capella, the bright star (a) upon the left shoulder of Auriga.
entries.notes: Links to the Sanskrit database entry brahmahridaya (Brahmahṛdaya = Capella).

entries.usage_note: The Arabic name that gives English 'Vega'. Its pair, nasru'ṭ-ṭāʼir 'the flying eagle', is Altair; Platts calls the dual nasrain 'the constellations of the Eagle and the Lyre'.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. nasr, p. 1138
entries.quote: A نسر nasr , s.m. A vulture; — an eagle: — nasruʼt̤-t̤āʼir, or nasr-ě-t̤āʼir, s.m. 'The flying eagle,' the constellation of the Eagle: — nasruʼl-wāqěʻ, s.m. 'The falling vulture,' the constellation of the Lyre.
entries.notes: confidence likely rather than certain because Platts glosses the terms as constellations (Lyra, Aquila) whereas in Arabic usage they name the bright stars Vega and Altair. name_native gives the headword نسر only; the compounds are printed in roman.

entries.usage_note: The source of English 'Altair'. Paired with nasru'l-wāqiʻ (Vega) as a dual, nasrain.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. nasr, p. 1138
entries.quote: nasruʼt̤-t̤āʼir, or nasr-ě-t̤āʼir, s.m. 'The flying eagle,' the constellation of the Eagle
entries.notes: Same caveat as Vega: Platts glosses it as the constellation, not the star.

entries.usage_note: The Persian image: the sky is streaked where someone dragged a bundle of straw across it. Fallon prints the Hindi equivalent akkās gaṅgā on the same line, which is exactly the two-layer situation this file is built to show. The image is shared with Arabic ṭarīqu't-tabn, 'the road of straw'.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. kahkashāṅ', p. 970
entries.quote: P کـﮩکشاں kahkashāṅ'; H. akkās gaṅgā; Sant. panjar, ḍahar , n. f. The milky way.
entries.notes: Platts files it under kāh, p. 808: 'kāh-kashān, s.m. The milky-way, galaxy'. Shakespear (1834) has it twice, pp. 1311 and 1408. Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), I. 25, glosses it 'the dragging of a bundle of straw through the sky'. The Santali forms in Fallon's line are not claimed here.

entries.usage_note: A folk name that answers to the Sanskrit Gajavīthī, 'the elephant's course' - Platts records gaj-vīthī for the Milky Way as well (p. 898) - but here it is built from the ordinary Hindi word hāthī, not from Sanskrit gaja.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. hāthī, p. 1215
entries.quote: hāthī-kī rāh, s.f. The galaxy or milky way (syn. ākāś-gaṅgā)
entries.notes: Headword printed by Platts as हाथी / هاتهي; the compound in roman only. Fallon, p. 1193, s.v. hāth'ī: 'hāthī kī rāh, akkās Gaṅgā, n. f. The milky way.'

entries.usage_note: The same 'road' image, but named for hathiyā, the thirteenth lunar mansion - the hand-shaped asterism in Corvus which in the Hindi belt is above all the season of the closing rains. A sky-road named after a calendar station, not after a bright star.
entries.citation: John Shakespear, A Dictionary, Hindustani and English, 3rd ed. (London, 1834), s.v. hath-iyā, p. 1851
entries.quote: هتهيا hath-iyā हस्त s. m. 1. The 13th mansion of the moon, Corvus. 2. The breaking up of the rains. هتهيا کي راه hathiyā kī rāh, The milky way.
entries.notes: Shakespear prints the Urdu script for both headword and compound; Platts, p. 1219, has it in roman under हथिया / هتهيا. Still recorded by McGregor, Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary (1993), p. 1057, s.v. हथिया.

entries.region: Punjab and northern India (contributed to a Panjab journal)
entries.usage_note: The colonial district court transposed to the sky - kachahrī is the ordinary word for a magistrate's court. Crooke picked this name up from the same source and reprinted it.
entries.citation: L. Whyte King, 'Names for the Milky Way', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Dec. 1884), note 308
entries.quote: Hindi : Akás Gangá ... Bhagwán kí Kachahrí, God's Court.
entries.notes: Quoted as printed apart from OCR noise in the diacritics. Repeated by Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), I. 25: 'The Hindu calls it Akash Ganga or the heavenly Ganges, Bhagwan ki kachahri or the Court of God, Swarga-duari or the door of Paradise.' Cited by note number, the standard locator for this journal.

entries.usage_note: Printed in the original note as 'Supesh Bidhi, the way of fate' and corrected by the contributor himself in a later note - a good example of why the correction slip matters.
entries.citation: L. Whyte King, 'Names for heavenly objects', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Feb. 1885), note 523, p. 84 (correcting note 308)
entries.quote: In notes 306 and 308, Vol. II, are some important misprints which are hereby corrected. ... 'Akás Gangá, the bed of the Ganges,' should be Akás Gangá, the Heavenly Ganges. 'Supesh Bidhi, the way of fate,' should be Sufed Badhi, the white garland.
entries.notes: confidence likely: the corrected form is attested only in this correction slip and its exact Hindi shape (bādhī? bāṛhī?) cannot be checked against a script form.

entries.usage_note: svarga 'heaven' + dvārī 'gateway', in vernacular shape. Crooke gives the same as Swarga-duari, 'the door of Paradise'.
entries.citation: R. C. Temple, 'Name for the Milky Way', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Mar. 1885), note 610, p. 102
entries.quote: Surg Dwárí, the Gate of Heaven: Hindi.
entries.notes: Corroborated by Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), I. 25-26.

entries.region: Multan and Dera Ghazi Khan (Multani/Saraiki, western Punjab)
entries.literal_meaning: 'the boat's track/fodder' - glossed by the contributor as 'The Path of (Noah's) Boat'
entries.usage_note: A Muslim-inflected version of the straw image: the Ark is dragged across the sky and leaves a wake. beṛā is the ordinary Punjabi word for a raft or boat; ghās, 'grass/fodder', keeps the Persian straw connection alive under a Qur'anic story.
entries.citation: A. Jukes, 'Name for the Milky Way', Panjab Notes and Queries, vol. II (Aug. 1885), note 1027, p. 194
entries.quote: In Multání or Derawál the Milky Way is called Berá dá Ghas, The Path of (Noah's) Boat.
entries.notes: confidence likely because the literal analysis of ghās here is the compiler's; the contributor gives only the free translation. Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), I. 26, repeats it as Panjabi: 'to the Panjabi it is known as Bera da ghas or the path of Noah's Ark'.

entries.usage_note: The Sanskrit name carried into Hindi with a vernacular first member (akkās for ākāśa). Recorded here because every other Milky Way name in this file is explicitly glossed against it - it is the reference point the folk names are measured from.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. ākās, p. 64
entries.quote: ākāś-gangā, s.f. The milky way (syn. kahkashāṅ)
entries.notes: Compound printed in roman under the headword आकास / آکاس. Links to the Sanskrit database entry akashaganga.

entries.usage_note: Named from the watch it belongs to: Platts's preceding sub-entry is ujāle-kā pahrā, 'the morning watch, the watch which begins at dawn'. The star is the one that stands in that watch.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. ujālā, p. 23
entries.quote: ujāle-kā tārā, s.m. The morning star, the planet Venus.
entries.notes: Headword printed as उजाला / اجالا; compound in roman only. Fallon, p. 37, s.v. ujā'lā, has the same.

entries.literal_meaning: 'the dawn one' (Platts derives it from S. vyuṣṭa 'daybreak'; cf. Hindi bhor 'dawn')
entries.usage_note: A purely vernacular formation on the word for daybreak, with no Sanskrit or Persian star name behind it.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. bhurkā, p. 186
entries.quote: H بهرکا भुरका bhurkā [S. व्युष्ट+कः], s.m. The morning star (cf. bhor).
entries.notes: Also Fallon, p. 304, s.v. bhur'kā. Platts's identification is 'the morning star' without naming Venus; the equation with Venus is secured by his own ujāle-kā tārā entry and by Fallon's.

entries.region: eastern Hindi belt (Fallon marks the sense 'morning star' E., the nose-ring sense W.)
entries.usage_note: The same word means both 'the morning star' and 'a gold star or patch fixed on a nose-ring' - the ornament/star doubling seen also in jhumkā and in Punjabi kirhkaṭī.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. bhalkā, p. 191
entries.quote: H بهلکا भलका bhalkā , s.m. Dawn of day, morning ( = bhor); the morning star (syn. bhurkā); a gold star or patch fixed on a nose-ring.
entries.notes: The regional split is Fallon's, p. 300: '1. (E). The morning star (bhurkā). 2. A gold star hanging in a nose-ring. W.'

entries.region: Punjab (contributed from Kasur by Ghulam Hussain Khan)
entries.literal_meaning: glossed by the contributor as 'the Galloping Star'
entries.usage_note: Named for motion: Venus visibly shifts against the stars faster than any other bright object, and the name records the observation.
entries.citation: Ghulam Hussain Khan, 'Panjab - Name for Venus - The Morning Star', Indian Notes and Queries, vol. IV (1886-87), note 363
entries.quote: A common name for the planet Venus or the Morning Star is in the Panjab Tapt Tárá, the Galloping Star, from its quick movement.
entries.notes: confidence likely: the first element is uncertain in the scanned type (Tapt / Ṭapaṭ) and the contributor's gloss 'galloping' does not obviously match Sanskrit tapta 'heated'; no script form is printed.

entries.usage_note: The standard Urdu name of the planet, from the same root as the compliment zǒhra-rū, 'Venus-faced'. Its Persian doublet is nāhīd (Platts p. 1120, from Avestan Anāhitā), and the Persian poets' irreverent name for it, lūlī-i-falak, 'heaven's dancing-girl', is also in Platts (p. 970).
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. zǒhra, p. 619
entries.quote: P زهره zǒhra (for A. زهرة zǒharat, v.n. fr. زهر 'to shine,' &c.), s.f. (m. ?), The planet Venus: — zǒhra-rū, adj. Like Venus in countenance.
entries.notes: The Panjab list in Panjab Notes and Queries II.521 (p. 84) confirms the split usage: 'Evening Star. Arabic: Zuhrah (evening); náhid, girl with swelling breasts. Persian: Lúlí-i-falak, heaven's fille de joie.'

entries.region: Hindustani generally; the proverb marked Hin. (Hindu usage) by Fallon
entries.usage_note: A tadbhava, not a tatsama: Prakrit sukko > Hindi sūk, which also names Friday. Fallon attaches a working rule to it - nothing auspicious is begun while Venus is set (i.e. during its heliocentric conjunction), a piece of practical astrology still observed at weddings.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. sūk, p. 794
entries.quote: H سوک सूक sūk; E. sukh; A. zohrā , n. m. S. शुक्र The planet Venus. Sūk ḍūbe shubh kāraj nahīṅ karte. Hin. When Venus sets no work should be done.
entries.notes: Platts has both suk (p. 663) and sūk (p. 699), each 'The planet Venus; — Friday'. Maya Singh, The Panjabi Dictionary (1895), p. 1075, gives Punjabi ਸੂਕ súk and p. 1076 ਸੁੱਕਰ sukkar for the same planet.

entries.usage_note: A comet is simply a broom in the sky. The word is otherwise heavily charged in domestic usage - Fallon records the women's curse 'may the broom sweep through your house' - which suits the omen value comets carried.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. jhāṛū, p. 400
entries.quote: H جهاڙو झाड़ू jhāṛū [rt. of jhāṛnā 'to sweep,'+ū = Prk. इडओ = S. (इ)तृ+कः], s.m. A broom, a besom, a whisk; — a comet
entries.notes: Also Fallon, p. 493, and Shakespear (1834), p. 653: 'A besom, broom, a comet.'

entries.region: Hindustani generally; the tail-star form marked dakh. (Deccani) by Shakespear
entries.usage_note: ket is the vernacular reduction of Sanskrit Ketu, the descending node and mythic tail; Fallon parses the word for his readers as 'lit. tail star', which is a folk etymology but tells us how it was heard. The transparent Hindustani phrase dum kā tārā says the same thing outright.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. ket, p. 980
entries.quote: H کيت केत ket; Sant. chanḍbol ipil , (lit. tail star), n. m. S. केतु A comet.
entries.notes: Shakespear (1834), p. 1996: 'دم کا تارا dum kā tārā, s. (dakh.) A comet (Harris)' - printed in the Urdu script and marked Deccani, like palang tīn cor. Platts (p. 526) has dum for a comet and (p. 527) the Persian sitāra-i-dumbāla-dār, 'a star having a tail'. Modern standard Hindi has पुच्छल तारा (McGregor 1993, p. 635).

entries.region: Punjab (contributed from Ambala by Chaina Mall)
entries.literal_meaning: 'the tailed star' (Indic and Perso-Arabic versions of the same phrase)
entries.usage_note: Both layers side by side in one sentence, with an attached practice: on the appearance of a comet subscriptions were raised and Brahmans and mendicants fed, because a comet foretold epidemic or famine.
entries.citation: Chaina Mall, 'Panjab - Comets', Indian Notes and Queries, vol. IV (1886-87), note 424
entries.quote: All over the Panjab people of all sorts dread the appearance of a puchhalwálá tárá, or dumdár sitárá, or tailed star; i. e., comet, as foreboding evil to the country in the shape of epidemic or famine.
entries.notes: Roman only in the source. Quoted with OCR noise in the diacritics normalised.

entries.usage_note: Qur'anic in origin - the shihāb thāqib hurled at eavesdropping jinn. Crooke found the word alive as a name for eerie lights in Rohilkhand and western Oudh, where the Shahaba over battlefield burial-grounds is a phantom army.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. shihāb, p. 738
entries.quote: A شہاب shihāb, vulg. shahāb (v.n. fr. شہب 'to be or become gray,' &c.), s.m. Flame (of fire); a firebrand; a brightly-shining star; a shooting or falling star; a meteor.
entries.notes: Fallon (p. 104) gives 'A. shahāb-i-sāqib' as the Arabic for Hindi ākās agan golā. For the will-o'-the-wisp sense see Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), II. 198.

entries.usage_note: A three-word descriptive compound, entirely vernacular in its material. Beside it Platts records the simple idiom tārā ṭūṭnā, 'a star to shoot' (p. 304), and the Hindi luk (p. 958, from S. ulkā) 'a fiery phenomenon in the sky; meteor; falling star'.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. ākās, p. 64
entries.quote: ākās-agan-gola, s.m. Meteor, shooting-star
entries.notes: Compound in roman only. On the beliefs attached: Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), I. 82, reports that a falling star means a great man's soul is passing through the air, and that people thrust five fingers into their mouths to keep their own souls from joining it.

modern_star.common_name: Gienah and the quadrilateral of Corvus
modern_star.bayer: γ Corvi (with α, β, δ, ε Corvi)

entries.region: eastern Hindi belt - Bhojpuri and Awadhi districts; Fallon's proverbs are marked Bhoj.
entries.usage_note: The single most important star name in Hindi-belt village life: not an object to look at but a rain season to reckon by. Grierson notes it is the longest of the asterisms, sixteen lunar days, and that cultivators said the rains used to end in Swati but now end in Hathiya. It is personified as Hathi rāni, 'Queen Hathiya', who announces herself by thunder.
entries.citation: S. W. Fallon, A New Hindustani-English Dictionary (Banaras/London, 1879), s.v. hath'iyā, p. 1197
entries.quote: ﮩتيا हथिया hath'iyā, hasth , n. m. S. हस्त The 13th mansion of the moon; Corvus. 1. Hathiyā barse tīn hot haiṅ, shakkar, shālī, māsh, Hathiyā barse tīn jāt haiṅ, tillī, kodo, kapās.
entries.notes: Fallon translates: 'When in the thirteenth mansion rain doth fall / Rice, sugarcane, and pulse, these three thrive all, / But cotton, kodo, sesamum, all three / The rains destroy beyond all remedy.' Grierson, Bihar Peasant Life (1885), §1082 p. 271 and §1084 p. 273, and §1090 pp. 281-82 for the Queen Hathiya couplet: 'Maggha lagáwe ghaggha, swáti láwas tati, / Kahtari Hathi rani, ham hun awat hati.' Platts, p. 1219, adds the second sense 'the end (or breaking up) of the rains'.

entries.region: Bihar (Bhojpuri/Magahi); the same forms in Fallon for Hindustani generally
entries.usage_note: The word survives in the countryside as a unit of the farming year, not of astronomy: twenty-seven unequal periods, each governing a specific operation, ranging from about thirteen lunar days in the dry months to sixteen for Hathiya. Grierson's list of their vernacular names - Rohni, Mirgsira, Aradra, Punarbas, Pukh, Maggha, Purba/Utra Phaguni, Hast or Hathiya, Chitra, Bināti or Siwāti, Bisākha, Anurādha, Jeshtha, Mul, Purba Khārh, Utra Khārh - is the vernacular register of the whole nakṣatra series in one place.
entries.citation: G. A. Grierson, Bihar Peasant Life (Calcutta, 1885), §1082, p. 271, with the table of asterisms pp. 272-73
entries.quote: Besides the above, another important division of the year must be noticed, — that into lunar asterisms (nakhat, nachhattr, or nichhattr). There are 27 of these in each year ... Each asterism is not of equal length. The longest is hathiya, which is 16 lunar days. ... Every agricultural operation commences in a certain asterism, and so it is necessary to know when they occur.
entries.notes: Grierson prints each name in Devanagari beside the transliteration, but the Devanagari is unrecoverable from the scanned text, so name_native is left null. Fallon, p. 1157, s.v. nichhat'tar, nachhattar (नछत्तर), gives the same generic word for Hindustani; Platts, p. 1148, notes the tatsama nakshatra with the vernacular naććhattar and 'corr. H. निक्षत्र nikshatr'.

entries.usage_note: Maya Singh prints the complete list of the twenty-seven (twenty-eight with Abhijit) under this headword in their Sanskrit forms, and notes that the Punjabi month names Māgh, Phaggun, Chet, Vaisākh, Jeth, Hār, Sāwan, Bhādroṅ, Assū, Kattak, Magar and Poh are derived from them. This is the entry that licenses the statement that Punjabi simply takes over the Sanskrit twenty-seven.
entries.citation: Bhai Maya Singh, The Panjabi Dictionary (Lahore, 1895), s.v. nachhattar, p. 786
entries.quote: NACHHATTAR ਨਛੱਤ੍ s. m. Corrupted from the Sanskrit word Nakshatra. A star, a horoscope; a lunar mansion or constellation in the moon's path; an asterism ... The names of various months are derived from these Nachhattars, thus Magh, Phaggun, Chet, Vaisakh, Jeth, Har, Sawan, Bhadron, Assu, Kattak, Magar and Poh.
entries.notes: This one entry stands for the whole Sanskrit twenty-seven in Punjabi; they are deliberately not itemised here.

entries.usage_note: Punjabi phonology on the Sanskrit name, with the gemination characteristic of the language. Maya Singh's first sense - a small earthen water-and-buttermilk pot - is a homonym, and shows the star name sitting inside ordinary domestic vocabulary.
entries.citation: Bhai Maya Singh, The Panjabi Dictionary (Lahore, 1895), s.v. magghá, p. 695
entries.quote: MAGGHÁ ਮੱਘਾ s. m. A small earthen vessel used for holding water and butter milk; the fifteenth of the twenty-seven (according to later reckoning twenty-eight) lunar mansions known to Hindu Astrology.
entries.notes: Maya Singh's ordinal 'fifteenth' counts from Śraviṣṭhā/Dhaniṣṭhā, as in his own list s.v. nachhattar; in the Aśvinī-first order Maghā is the tenth. In Bihar the same asterism appears as Maggha in the rain proverbs (Grierson 1885, p. 281).

entries.usage_note: Attached to a Punjabi weather proverb, which is what makes it more than a transliteration: the brighter Rohṇī shows on the eleventh of the dark half of Sāwan, the better the harvest.
entries.citation: Bhai Maya Singh, The Panjabi Dictionary (Lahore, 1895), s.v. rohṉí, p. 971
entries.quote: ROHṈÍ ਰੋਹਣੀ s. m. The fourth lunar mansion, which comprises Aldebaran and four other stars in Taurus:—Sáwaṉ badí ekádsí, joṭhí rohṉí hoe, etá samá parakhye maṉ báṇchhat phal hoi.
entries.notes: Maya Singh translates: 'Understand that the more the star Rohṇí shows on the eleventh dark half of Sáwaṉ, the more there will be produce to delight your heart.—Prov.' The 'four other stars in Taurus' are the Hyades; cf. Sanskrit database entry rohini-shakata, the Wain of Rohiṇī.

entries.usage_note: The workhorse word, and the base of most compound names in this file (guććhā tārā, quṭbī tārā, ujāle-kā tārā, dhurū tārā, dum kā tārā, tapt tārā). Platts's sub-entries are a small ethnography in themselves: tārā ṭūṭnā 'a star to shoot', tāre ginnā 'to count the stars, to get no sleep', tāroṅ-kī chān 'daybreak', din-ko tāre dikhānā 'to show one stars by daylight, to beat severely'.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. tārā, p. 304
entries.quote: H تارا तारा tārā [S. तार (for स्तार)+कं; and S. तारा fem.], s.m. A star; planet; falling star, meteor; the pupil of the eye
entries.notes: Punjabi ਤਾਰਾ tárá, 'A star', in Maya Singh (1895), p. 1106.

entries.usage_note: The Persian counterpart of tārā, cognate with it through Indo-Iranian - Platts gives the etymology explicitly. It carries the fortune-telling vocabulary: sitāra-shinās 'astrologer', sitāra chamaknā 'for one's star to shine'. Alongside it Urdu has Arabic najm and kaukab and Persian aḵẖtar, all glossed simply 'a star; constellation'.
entries.citation: John T. Platts, A Dictionary of Urdu, Classical Hindi and English (London, 1884), s.v. sitāra, p. 637
entries.quote: P ستاره sitāra [Pārsī śtār, śtāra; Pehl. śtār, śtārak; Zend śtare; S. स्तर्], s.m. A star; fortune, fate, destiny ... sitāre-o-burj, s.m. The constellations and the fixed stars.
entries.notes: aḵẖtar at Platts p. 29, najm at p. 1125, kaukab at p. 863; burj, 'a sign of the zodiac; asterism, constellation', at p. 145, and in Punjabi as ਬੁਰਜ burj (Maya Singh 1895, p. 174).

entries.name_roman: (the stars as kine, the moon their shepherd)
entries.usage_note: Not a name but a cosmology, transmitted by women to children, and the closest thing in this material to a systematic non-Sanskritic picture of the night sky.
entries.citation: W. Crooke, 'Kine as Stars', North Indian Notes and Queries, vol. IV (1894-95), note 279
entries.quote: Native women are very fond of telling their children that the stars are kine and the moon their shepherd.
entries.notes: Crooke repeats it in The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), I. 25. No vernacular wording is recorded, so name_roman is descriptive.

caveats: NO RAJASTHANI ENTRY IS CLAIMED. Despite the source group's title, not one Marwari or Rajasthani star name could be verified from a public-domain printed source with a page reference. Panjab, Indian and North Indian Notes and Queries (1883-96) carry no Rajputana star note; Fallon's Māṛ. (Marwari) tags never fall on a sky word; Maya Singh covers Punjabi only. The standard Rajasthani lexicon (Sitaram Lalas, Rājasthānī Sabad Kos) is in copyright and was not consulted. This is a real gap in the file, not evidence that Rajasthani lacks such names.

The `register` field is an analytic judgement by the compiler, not a label found in the sources. `sanskritic` is used for both tatsama forms (dhruv-tārā, ākāś-gaṅgā) and tadbhava reflexes in vernacular phonology (sūk < Śukra, kirhkaṭī < Kṛttikā, rohṇī, magghā); `vernacular` is used mainly for the Perso-Arabic astronomical vocabulary naturalised through Urdu; `folk` for names a dictionary or ethnographer flags as colloquial, rural, proverbial or metaphorical. Boundary cases (agast, ket, hathiyā, nakhat) are Sanskrit words that have become folk-calendrical property, and are tagged `folk` because that is how the sources use them.

No entry in this file is tagged `tribal`. Fallon systematically supplies Santali equivalents (Ursa Major buṛhī parkom, Milky Way panjar / ḍahar, comet chanḍbol ipil) and they are quoted in the notes where they occur, but Santali is Munda, outside the four languages of this source group, and no entry is claimed on that basis.

Script discipline: Platts prints Devanagari beside the Urdu script only for words he classes H (Hindi) or S (Sanskrit); for A (Arabic) and P (Persian) headwords he prints the Urdu script alone. Nearly all the interesting folk names are sub-entries printed in transliteration only - in those cases `name_native` is null rather than back-transliterated. Where Devanagari and the Urdu script are both given the Devanagari is placed first, separated by a slash. The printed originals of Platts, Fallon and Shakespear use Nastaʿlīq; the DSAL digital text renders it in naskh, and that is what is reproduced here.

Notes and Queries citations give the volume and the numbered note, which is the standard and unambiguous locator for these journals; a printed page is added where the running head was legible in the scan. The scanned OCR of these volumes garbles diacritics badly, and quotations from them have been normalised in the diacritics only - wording and word order are as printed. Where a reading is uncertain the entry says so in `confidence`.

Fallon (1879) glosses Arabic suhail as 'the dog star', i.e. Sirius. This is an error - Shakespear (1834), Platts (1884) and Fallon's own agas'ti entry all give Canopus. No independent Hindi, Urdu or Punjabi name for SIRIUS was found anywhere in these sources, and none is claimed. Likewise no vernacular name was found for Antares, the Hyades as a separate group, or Cassiopeia.

Fallon (p. 115) offers 'H. nāo' (boat) as the Hindi for Argo Navis. That looks like a lexicographer's translation of the Latin constellation name rather than an attested folk usage, so it is deliberately excluded from the entries.

McGregor's Oxford Hindi-English Dictionary (1993), Bahri (1989) and Caturvedi (1970) are in copyright. They were consulted to check which of these names survive into modern standard Hindi - kacpaciyā/kacpacī, hathiyā kī rāh, quṭub, suhel, pucchal tārā all do - but they are cited in `notes` only and never quoted.

Several names are attested for one sky object by more than one source with divergent regional marking: palang tīn cor, dum kā tārā and gagan ke bacce-wālī murġī are marked dakh. (Deccani) by Shakespear in 1834 but appear unmarked in Platts and Fallon fifty years later, which may mean northern spread, or may mean only that Platts and Fallon did not mark their sources. Both readings are left open.

The Panjabi Great Bear divides differently from the Hindustani one: Dames records the four bowl stars and the three handle stars under separate names (palang-pāwe, traṅgaṛ) in Jhang, while O'Brien's Multani Glossary makes traṅgar the whole constellation. Both are entered, with the disagreement stated.
